[PMID 42364973 | PMC13310184 full text via pmc_xml] PBPK Modeling and Clinical Data Reveal Reduced Impact of CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 Inhibitors on Elimination of Siponimod. :: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the leading cause of neurological disability among young adults and is the predominant disorder that causes demyelination in the central nervous system [1]. It often manifests as relapsing types, such as relapsing–remitting MS (RRMS) or secondary progressive MS (SPMS) [2].
Currently, a considerable medical need remains to find therapies that will be effective in delaying disability progression in patients with SPMS [2]. Siponimod is a potent and orally administered modulator that specifically targets sphingosine‐1‐phosphate (S1P) receptors [3]. It selectively attaches to two out of the five known G protein–coupled receptors on lymphocytes, consequently hindering their exit from lymph nodes. This reduces the recirculation of T cells into the central nervous system, resulting in reduced central inflammation [4, 5]. Siponimod is approved in more than 80 countries for the treatment of relapsing–remitting MS and active secondary progressive MS [6]. The polymorphic enzyme CYP2C9 is the major metabolizing enzyme for siponimod (79.3%), followed by CYP3A4 (18.5%), in subjects with the CYP2C9*1*1 genotype (extensive metabolizers) according to in vitro enzyme phenotyping data [7, 8]. The maintenance dose of siponimod in patients with CYP2C9 genotypes *1*1, *1*2 and *2*2 is 2 mg once daily and 1 mg for *3*3 and *2*3. The different genotypes require different titration when starting treatment with siponimod (Table S2).
Based on these fractional enzyme contributions to siponimod clearance (CL), physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling indicated a differential CYP2C9 genotype‐dependent inhibition and induction of CPY3A4 pathways [9]. PBPK simulations using Simcyp predicted a 18% and 31% increase in siponimod AUC when co‐administered with the CYP3A4 inhibitor itraconazole (100 mg b.i.d), in *1*2 and *1*3 subjects, respectively, as expected for a fraction metabolized via CYP3A4 (fm, CYP3A4) of 18.5% in wild‐type CYP2C9 subjects [10]. However, co‐administration of siponimod 0.25 mg with itraconazole (100 mg b.i.d) resulted in a 10% and 24% decrease in area under the concentration‐time curve (AUC) in the healthy subjects with the CYP2C9*1*2 and *1*3 genotypes, respectively, indicating a possible influence of the CYP2C9 genotype on the effect of itraconazole. To confirm the effect of other strong and selective CYP3A4 inhibitors on siponimod exposure and estimate the in vivo fraction metabolized by CYP3A4, a clinical DDI study with clarithromycin was conducted. Clarithromycin is a potent and selective CYP3A4 inhibitor which is expected to increase siponimod exposure in CYP2C9 intermediate metabolizers *1*3. The clinical impact of strong and selective CYP3A4 inhibitors like clarithromycin on siponimod exposure has previously been predicted by a PBPK model which used the fraction metabolized (fm), CYP3A4 determined by the in vitro enzyme phenotype study of 18.5% [9]. [PMID 42591558 | PMC13462044 full text via pmc_xml] Physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling of fluconazole: interpretation of gender-dependent pharmacokinetics and cytochrome P450 inhibition. :: Drug–drug interaction (DDI) occurs when a substrate drug is coadministered with another drug that acts as an inhibitor or inducer. Depending on the contribution of such metabolizing enzymes and transporters to the substrate drugs, the interactions can change plasma levels, potentially resulting in clinically significant effects, labeling restrictions, or unfavorable outcomes of the drug (Neuvonen et al., 1998; Niemi et al., 2003). For example, plasma exposure of simvastatin (40 mg single dose on day 4), an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor, was increased 19-fold in both the area under the plasma concentration–time curve (AUC) to infinity (AUCinf) and maximum concentration (Cmax) in healthy volunteers by itraconazole (200 mg daily for 4 days), a well-known cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 inhibitor (Neuvonen et al., 1998). The complete inhibition of CYP3A by itraconazole led to a tremendous increase in simvastatin exposure, leading to an increase in the potential risk of adverse effects, such as rhabdomyolysis. Niemi et al. (2003) evaluated the possible DDI of gemfibrozil, a fibrate drug to manage hypertriglyceridemia, with repaglinide, which is used to lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, and found that the AUCinf and Cmax of repaglinide (0.25 mg single dose on day 3) were increased 8.1- and 2.4-fold, respectively, by gemfibrozil coadministration (600 mg twice daily for 3 days). The higher plasma exposure of repaglinide by gemfibrozil may increase the risk of hypoglycemia. Repaglinide is a substrate of CYP2C8 and OATP1B1; dual inhibitory mechanisms can explain the greater DDI effects between repaglinide and gemfibrozil. These examples underscore the importance of identifying precise DDI mechanisms to avoid the undesired drug effects.
Fluconazole is a bis-triazole derivative developed for the treatment of superficial and systemic fungal infections, which predominantly affect immunocompromised individuals (Debruyne and Ryckelynck, 1993). It is a potent CYP2C9 inhibitor with an in vitro inhibition constant (Ki) value of 7–8 µM (Kunze et al., 1996) and can moderately inhibit CYP2C9 at clinically relevant doses. As a potent CYP2C19 inhibitor (Ki = 2 μM) (Wienkers et al., 1996), fluconazole could enhance the effects of proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole (Kang et al., 2002). Fluconazole is also a moderate inhibitor of CYP3A (Gibbs et al., 1999), with inhibitory effects weaker than those of itraconazole. Fluconazole has been shown to elevate exposure to statins, benzodiazepines, calcium channel blockers, and immunosuppressants, thereby raising risks such as myopathy, sedation, hypotension, and toxicity (Canafax et al., 1991; Hylton Gravatt et al., 2017; Kremens et al., 1999; Ulivelli et al., 2004). Additionally, it inhibits CYP3A5 (Gibbs et al., 1999), though to a lesser extent than CYP3A4, contributing to variability in drug metabolism. paragraphs.text: Using the updated model, siponimod net AUC ratios ranging from 0.27 to 0.39 were predicted for the CYP2C9*1*1, *1*2, *1*3, *2*2, and *2*3 genotypes for the strong CYP3A4/moderate CYP2C9 inducer rifampicin. For the moderate CYP3A4 inducer efavirenz, siponimod was predicted to show no to weak induction effects, with net AUC ratios between 0.64 and 1.03. Therefore, strong CYP3A4 inducers should be avoided, and moderate CYP3A4 inducers should be used with caution.

The dose titration of siponimod is a necessary step to desensitize the S1P1 receptors in the heart, being most critical at treatment day 1. Using PBPK modeling, it was demonstrated that there is little difference between the C max values across CYP2C9 genotypes for the first day of treatment (Figure 4), which is considered most relevant for the desensitization with regard to cardiac safety at treatment initiation. Even in the presence of fluconazole, which represents the worst case DDI scenario for siponimod with the highest net DDI effect of CYP inhibitors, little difference in the C max concentrations across genotypes was predicted for the first day.

For the four CYP inhibitors, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, erythromycin, and fluconazole, the DDI simulations with siponimod were performed (Table S12). The maximal predicted exposure increase (excluding genotype CYP2C9*3*3) was 1.12 for the genotype CYP2C9*2*3 with the strong CYP3A4 inhibitor ketoconazole and 1.88 for CYP2C9 wild type for the dual moderate CYP2C9/CYP3A4 inhibitor fluconazole. Calculation of the net DDI effect based on AUC factoring in the genotype‐specific exposure and the genotype‐specific dose (Table 2). The net AUC ratios were close to 1 for the CYP3A4 inhibitors clarithromycin, ketoconazole, and erythromycin and ranging from 1.66 to 2.20 for the moderate CYP2C9/CYP3A4 inhibitor fluconazole across genotypes.

With fluconazole, a limited DDI effect was predicted with a maximal siponimod AUC ratio of 1.88 for CYP2C9 wild type. [PMID 42888416 | PMC13675977 full text via pmc_xml] CYP3A and CYP2D6 variability in antimalarial pharmacokinetics and pharmacogenetics across populations: a narrative review. :: Research into the pharmacokinetics and pharmacogenetics of antimalarial agents is increasingly recognised as a vital, though still developing, area within malaria research. Key uncertainties remain around mechanisms of action, tolerability, adverse reactions, and drug-drug interactions [1, 2], all of which can differ across populations [3–6]. Treating Plasmodium falciparum malaria, often life-threatening if left untreated, carries a heightened risk of drug-related side effects. In the context of travel medicine, these adverse reactions are a major factor in poor adherence to chemoprophylaxis among travellers in endemic regions [7, 8]. Such lapses in adherence contribute to malaria incidence placing travellers at risk of severe disease and even death.
Looking ahead, a central goal for malaria therapy and prevention would be to tailor antimalarial regimens more closely to individual metabolic profiles, adjusting doses accordingly, or to design new agents with improved tolerability [6, 9].
This review aims to provide an overview of the pharmacokinetics, pharmacogenetics, and distribution of genetic variants of relevant cytochrome P450 (CYP) genes across different populations that may influence the efficacy of different antimalarial drugs, offering clinicians insights into the potential implications.
Previous reviews have summarised the pharmacogenetics of antimalarial drugs and CYP pharmacogenes [6, 10]. However, this review provides an updated and clinically focused synthesis by integrating recent evidence on CYP3A4, CYP3A5, and CYP2D6 with population allele distributions, pregnancy, HIV and tuberculosis co-treatment, and recently published studies through June 2026, including dolutegravir co-administration and tafenoquine.
A wide range of antimalarial agents, whether used preventively or for treatment, are metabolised through the human cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme network [3, 4, 6]. Among the CYP enzymes involved in antimalarial drug metabolism, CYP3A4, CYP3A5, CYP2D6, CYP2C8, CYP2C19, CYP2A6, and CYP1A2 are particularly relevant. This review focuses on CYP3A4, CYP3A5, and CYP2D6, for which the strongest pharmacogenetic evidence is currently available [6].
This system consists of membrane-associated haemoproteins with catalytic activity and multiple isoenzymes [11, 12]. CYP enzymes are mixed-function monooxygenases that primarily catalyse the oxidation of lipophilic compounds, thereby increasing their water solubility and promoting their elimination from the body [11]. CYP enzymes catalyse phase I biotransformation reactions, including hydrolysis, dealkylation, deamination, and oxidation, thereby facilitating the metabolism of both endogenous molecules and xenobiotics [6, 11].
Of the 57 known functional human CYP genes, members of CYP families 1, 2 and 3 are particularly important for drug metabolism, with roughly a dozen CYP enzymes accounting for the metabolism of nearly 80% of clinically used drugs [6, 11, 13].

paragraphs.text: Allelic analysis of CYP2D6 showed a predominance of alleles associated with normal enzymatic activity (*1 and *2, at 34.7% and 25.8%, respectively). Alleles related to intermediate/poor metabolizers (*9, *10, *17, and *41) were observed in both groups, ranging between 2.5 and 6.8%, whereas alleles with null function (*3, *4, and *5) were less frequent (0.4–5.9%), with *5 notable for 3.8% gene deletions (Table 3). A relevant finding was the significant difference in the frequency of the *39 allele between groups, being more prevalent in participants treated with PQ (10.4%) compared to those treated with TQ (1.0%; P = 0.002).

The predicted phenotype was predominantly normal metabolizers (gNM), representing 76.3% of the participants, followed by intermediate/poor metabolizers (gIM + gPM), which accounted for 23.7%. No ultrarapid metabolizers (gUM) were identified in this study (Table 3).

Among participants who experienced recurrence until D180, there were distinct allelic frequency patterns as observed between the TQ and PQ treatment groups. In the TQ case group, the *1 and *2 alleles (associated with normal enzymatic activity) were the most frequent at 40.6% and 21.9%, respectively, while in the TQ control group, they were 35.7% and 34.3%, respectively. The intermediate/poor metabolizer alleles *3, *4, and *5 were present at 9.4% and 3.1% in the case group, and 1.4%, 2.9%, and 1.4% in the control group, respectively (Table 4).

Concerning the participants treated with PQ, *1 and *2 allele frequencies were 31.1% and 16.2% in the case group, and 35.0% and 30.0% in the control group, respectively. Alleles *4 and *5 were found at 9.5% and 6.8% in the case group, and both at 3.3% in the control group (Table 4). The most frequent phenotype was normal metabolizer, accounting for 82.4% of those treated with TQ and 71.6% of those treated with PQ. No statistically significant difference was found between the treatment groups (P = 0.172).

[PMID 41104340 | PMC12521184 full text via pmc_xml] Pharmacogenomics of antibiotic-induced hypersensitivity reactions: current evidence and implications in clinical practice. :: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are gradually becoming a concerning health threat worldwide in patients undergoing acute or chronic therapy (Osanlou et al., 2018). Rawlins and Thompson grouped ADRs into two types: dose-dependent and predictable reactions (type A) and unpredictable dose-independent reactions (type B) (Dekker et al., 1997). Hypersensitivity reaction, a type-B ADR, is produced by cellular mediators released through both immunological and non-immune mechanisms (Doña et al., 2012). Allergic reactions are hypersensitivity reactions involving either an immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated or non-IgE (e.g., T cell)-mediated mechanism (Johansson et al., 2004). Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs) are potentially fatal T-cell-mediated delayed allergic reactions (Peter et al., 2017). The most prevalent SCARs, contributing to over 85% of the SCARs occurring in adults, are drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS), toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) (Duong et al., 2017; Sassolas et al., 2010).
A high estimated mortality ranging from 10% to 40% for SJS/TEN, <5% for AGEP and 2%–10% for DRESS was reported (Chen et al., 2010; Duong et al., 2017; Firoz et al., 2012; Husain et al., 2013; Kloypan et al., 2021; Owen and Jones, 2021; Schneck et al., 2008). Globally, the prevalence of SCARs was said to be 0.4–1.2 per million/years (Verma et al., 2013). Nevertheless, a racial discrepancy in the prevalence of SCARs has also been recorded. For example, the incidence was reported to be as high as 1.53–1.89 per million/year in the German population, whereas among the Filipino population, the rate of SCARs was reported to be 6.25/10,000 people from 2011 to 2015 (Guzman and Paliza, 2018; Mockenhaupt, 2012; Tempark et al., 2022). Additionally, the prevalence of TEN and SJS was estimated to be 0.4–1.2 and 1-6 per million/year, respectively, among the European population, while the rate was 0.94–1.45 and 3.96–5.03 per million/year, respectively, for Koreans (Yang et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2021; Duong et al., 2017).
Antibiotics are the main drugs that cause immune-mediated ADRs, such as SCARs, allergic reactions, and organ-specific diseases, representing an indisputable threat to patient safety (Blumenthal et al., 2019). [PMID 42524757 | PMC13519768 full text via pmc_xml] MT-RNR1 genotype testing for preventing aminoglycoside-mediated ototoxicity: A guideline developed by the UK Centre of Excellence in Regulatory Science and Innovation in Pharmacogenomics (CERSI-PGx). :: Aminoglycosides are natural or semisynthetic antibiotics derived from the filamentous bacteria Actinomycetes. They were among the first antibiotics to be introduced for routine clinical use, and several examples have been approved for use in humans. Streptomycin was the first drug in class licenced for the treatment of tuberculosis in the 1940s. Following this, other members of the drug class, including neomycin, kanamycin, gentamicin, netilmicin, tobramycin and amikacin were developed. 1 Even though they are effective antimicrobials, their side effect profiles and the need for therapeutic drug monitoring led to a shift towards alternative agents. With the increasing emergence of multidrug resistance, the use of aminoglycosides has increased, and recently novel aminoglycosides have been developed, including arbekacin and plazomicin. 1
The side effect profiles are similar across the antibiotic class, with both nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity recognized complications, with up to 17% of individuals experiencing ototoxicity following intravenous administration of aminoglycosides. 2 , 3 Dosing regimens and therapeutic drug monitoring have been used to reduce aminoglycoside toxicity (especially nephrotoxicity) while maintaining their effectiveness. Now a once‐daily, high‐dose regimen approach is accepted as the preferred standard administration. 4 However, ototoxicity remains unpredictable and may occur at therapeutic concentrations.
Aminoglycosides bind to the tRNA binding site of 16S ribosomal RNA in the 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes, disrupting mRNA translation, causing accumulation of truncated and dysfunctional proteins, which kill sensitive bacteria. 5 They are active against various Gram‐positive and Gram‐negative organisms, especially members of the Enterobacteriaceae family, including Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. 1 The class has activity against Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin‐resistant and vancomycin‐resistant strains. They are used to treat Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Mycobacterium species, including extensive drug‐resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the management of non‐tuberculous mycobacterial infection, for example, Mycobacterium avium and Mycobacterium abscessus. This broad‐spectrum activity of aminoglycosides is enhanced through synergy with other classes of antimicrobials, especially beta‐lactams. 6
In 1993, a variant m.1555A > G in the mitochondrial DNA encoded gene MT‐RNR1 was associated with increased susceptibility to sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) following exposure to aminoglycosides. 7 Subsequent studies have identified additional variants in MT‐RNR1 (m.1095 T > C and m.1494C > T), which also predispose to aminoglycoside induced hearing loss (AIHL). These variants are found at different frequencies across different biogeographical groups (Table 1). 8 In combination, the frequency of these variants is approximately 1 in 330 individuals.

[PMID 42919487 | PMC13694199 full text via pmc_xml] Stereoselective Determination of Omeprazole and 5-Hydroxy-Omeprazole in Dried Blood Spots for CYP2C19 Activity Assessment. :: Phenoconversion represents a major limitation to genotype‐guided therapy, as it results in clinically relevant misclassification of metaboliser status despite accurate genotyping. Therefore, a preferable approach may be to directly measure patient‐specific enzyme activity by quantifying the concentrations of an enzyme‐specific probe drug and its metabolite, referred to as drug phenotyping [1, 2]. Besides its potential clinical utility, phenotype measurements can contribute to identifying relevant phenoconversion sources and estimating its impact in clinical practice. However, the performance of drug phenotyping exhibits considerable variability, with measurements demonstrating a range of precision across different contexts and methodologies [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Unaccounted methodological limitations of phenotyping may therefore lead to over‐ or underestimation of enzyme activity and phenoconversion rates, limiting its application in research or clinical practice.
Phenotyping approaches may be particularly beneficial for estimating CYP2C19 activity, as this enzyme is frequently associated with phenoconversion [8, 9, 10, 11]. Currently, a single dose of 10–20 mg omeprazole (OME) is the most utilised in vivo CYP2C19 phenotyping probe, offering broad availability, minimal toxicity, and high correlation with S‐mephenytoin 5‐hydroxylation, suggesting specificity for CYP2C19 [12, 13, 14]. OME comprises a racemic mixture of R‐ and S‐enantiomers with stereoselective pharmacokinetics (PK). Figure 1 depicts the stereoselective 5‐hydroxylation (5‐OH) pathways underlying its use as a CYP2C19 phenotyping probe [15, 16, 21, 22].
Stereoselective 5‐hydroxylation (5‐OH) pathways of omeprazole (OME) when administered as a racemic mixture. A small clinical study reported no significant influence of strong CYP3A4 inhibition on the 5‐OH‐OME/OME ratio [25], but human liver microsomes have suggested the opposite, with up to 40%–50% contribution of CYP3A4 to 5‐hydroxylation with changing OME or enzyme availability [16, 26]. [PMID 42844533] (Clinical pharmacokinetics, 2026) Assessing the Influence of CYP3A4 Inhibitors on Voriconazole Exposure across CYP2C19 Genotypes: A Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Model Analysis. Voriconazole (VCZ) is a triazole antifungal agent used to treat invasive infections. It has narrow therapeutic index and exhibits high interindividual variability due to cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 autoinhibition and CYP2C19 polymorphism. As VCZ is a CYP3A4 substrate, it is susceptible to drug-drug interactions (DDIs) with CYP3A4 inhibitors, resulting in increased VCZ exposure. However, due to the differences in CYP2C19 activity, the fraction of VCZ metabolized by CYP3A4 varies across CYP2C19 genotypes. As a result, coadministration of CYP3A4 inhibitors could result in genotype-dependent increases in VCZ exposure, leading to a disproportionate risk for toxicity across genotypes. Despite this, the clinical impact of CYP3A4 inhibition on VCZ exposure across different CYP2C19 genotypes remains poorly characterized. The purpose of this study was to develop a genotype-specific VCZ physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model to assess the impact of CYP3A4 inhibition and CYP2C19 polymorphism on VCZ exposure. A genotype-specific VCZ PBPK model was developed and evaluated in PK-Sim® using observed VCZ pharmacokinetic and DDI data. VCZ-CYP3A4 inhibitor DDI potential was assessed by comparing model predicted VCZ exposure with or without CYP3A4 inhibitors across CYP2C19 genotypes. Due to VCZ's CYP3A4 autoinhibition, DDI potential was assessed following single doses of VCZ and at steady state. [PMID 42933756] (Environmental research, 2026) Systematic Evaluation and Machine Learning-Based Driver Analysis of Cadmium-Induced Osteotoxicity in Mammals. Cadmium (Cd) is a persistent environmental pollutant with a biological half-life of several decades in animals. However, the osteotoxic effects in the mammalian skeletal system and their underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using 374 control-observation comparisons from 47 studies, we systematically evaluated Cd-associated skeletal toxicity through meta-analysis and machine learning. The results indicate that Cd exposure significantly impairs overall bone health (13.68%, P < 0.001). TRACP5b (61.52%, P < 0.001) and CTX-I (35.29%, P < 0.01) showed the strongest responses, whereas BMD (10.28%, P < 0.001) and body weight (6.06%, P < 0.001) changed more moderately. TRACP5b responded approximately sixfold more strongly than BMD, supporting bone resorption markers as more sensitive early-warning indicators of Cd-induced skeletal toxicity. The XGBoost model demonstrated the best performance on the test set (R2 = 0.752, RMSE = 0.325), highlighting its strong potential for predicting Cd-induced bone toxicity risk. SHAP analysis identified response indicators (9.5%-23.3%) and Cd concentration plus duration (18%) as major contributors to osteotoxic response variation. Biologically, these findings indicate that Cd-associated osteotoxicity is characterized by heterogeneous sensitivity across bone-remodeling endpoints, while exposure concentration and duration modulate the magnitude of this multi-target skeletal response. These findings provide a basis for refining cadmium risk assessment and screening early-warning biomarkers.
[PMID 42886207] (Pharmacogenomics, 2026) Pharmacogenetics in HIV therapy: a review of key biomarkers, regulatory annotations, and clinical dosing guidelines. Pharmacogenetics is pivotal in modern HIV management, facilitating the transition from the traditional "one-size-fits-all" model toward personalized precision medicine. By analyzing how unique genetic profiles influence pharmacological responses, clinicians can maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing toxicities and adverse drug reactions. Given the high interindividual variability in antiretroviral drug exposure and the necessity for lifelong treatment, identifying key genetic biomarkers is essential to optimize patient safety, treatment adherence, and overall quality of life. This narrative review evaluates major gene-drug associations in HIV therapy, focusing on HLA-B * 57:01 for abacavir, UGT1A1 for atazanavir and dolutegravir, and CYP2B6 for efavirenz. The research includes an exhaustive review of pharmacogenomic databases (e.g. ClinPGx), regulatory agency labels (FDA, EMA, Swissmedic, HC-SC, PMDA), and clinical guidelines from CPIC and DPWG. Integrating pharmacogenetics into clinical practice significantly improves patient safety and treatment adherence. While HLA-B * 57:01 screening is widely implemented, barriers remain for other markers, including logistical challenges and the lack of genomic representation for African and Latin American populations. Clinicians must utilize evidence-based resources and remain updated on this evolving field to effectively tailor antiretroviral regimens and practice precision medicine.

Depending on the contribution of such metabolizing enzymes and transporters to the substrate drugs, the interactions can change plasma levels, potentially resulting in clinically significant effects, labeling restrictions, or unfavorable outcomes of the drug (Neuvonen et al., 1998; Niemi et al., 2003). For example, plasma exposure of simvastatin (40 mg single dose on day 4), an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor, was increased 19-fold in both the area under the plasma concentration–time curve (AUC) to infinity (AUCinf) and maximum concentration (Cmax) in healthy volunteers by itraconazole (200 mg daily for 4 days), a well-known cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 inhibitor (Neuvonen et al., 1998). The complete inhibition of CYP3A by itraconazole led to a tremendous increase in simvastatin exposure, leading to an increase in the potential risk of adverse effects, such as rhabdomyolysis. Niemi et al. (2003) evaluated the possible DDI of gemfibrozil, a fibrate drug to manage hypertriglyceridemia, with repaglinide, which is used to lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, and found that the AUCinf and Cmax of repaglinide (0.25 mg single dose on day 3) were increased 8.1- and 2.4-fold, respectively, by gemfibrozil coadministration (600 mg twice daily for 3 days). The higher plasma exposure of repaglinide by gemfibrozil may increase the risk of hypoglycemia. Repaglinide is a substrate of CYP2C8 and OATP1B1; dual inhibitory mechanisms can explain the greater DDI effects between repaglinide and gemfibrozil. These examples underscore the importance of identifying precise DDI mechanisms to avoid the undesired drug effects.

Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is widely used in lupus nephritis (LN), but interindividual variability in pharmacokinetics and pharmacogenetics may affect treatment response. This study investigated the relationship between MMF pharmacokinetics, key genetic polymorphisms, and therapeutic response in Egyptian female LN patients. In this prospective study, 53 female patients with active LN (ISN/RPS class III-IV) maintained on 2 g/day MMF were enrolled at the Urology and Nephrology Center, Mansoura University, Egypt. Baseline clinical, laboratory, and histopathological data were collected. Serial blood samples were obtained over 8 h for mycophenolic acid (MPA) quantification by LC/MS. Genomic DNA was extracted for UGT2B7 (rs7438135) and SLCO1B1 (rs183624077) genotyping using TaqMan real-time PCR assays. Treatment response was classified as complete or partial remission versus non-response at 6 months. Population pharmacokinetics were analyzed using Monolix 2020R1. Considerable variability in MPA exposure was observed (mean AUC₀-₈: 22.4 ± 12.9 µg·h/mL; mean Cmax: 12.9 ± 5.5 µg/mL). Responders exhibited higher median AUC₀-₈ than non-responders (23.1 vs. 16.2 µg·h/mL; p = 0.039). SLCO1B1 and UGT2B7 genotypes did not differ significantly between responders and non-responders, though TT carriers showed lower MPA AUC₀-₈. Multivariate analysis identified biopsy class (III vs. IV), induction therapy with MMF, and higher MPA AUC₀-₈ as independent predictors of response. MMF exposure, biopsy class, and induction regimen significantly influence therapeutic response in LN. Pharmacokinetic monitoring of MPA may help optimize MMF therapy, while common UGT2B7 and SLCO1B1 variants showed limited predictive value in this cohort.

[PMID 41286971 | PMC12642190 full text via pmc_xml] Fetal posterior cerebral artery infarction due to carotid dissection: a case report. :: In a typical circle of Willis configuration, cerebral perfusion is supplied by two interconnected arterial systems. The vertebrobasilar system ensures blood supply of the posterior circulation via two vertebral arteries merging into a single basilar artery, which ends in two posterior cerebral arteries. Further, the anterior circulation is supported by two internal carotid arteries (ICA) whose terminal branches are the anterior and middle cerebral arteries [1]. The circle of Willis is an anastomotic circle where the anterior and posterior circulation are interconnected via the posterior communicating arteries (PComA) that link the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and ICA.
Fetal posterior cerebral artery (FPCA) is an anatomical variant occurring in 23–29% of the population unilaterally and 1–9% bilaterally [2]. In FPCA, P2 portion of PCA emerges from PComA, while the P1 portion of PCA is usually hypoplastic or atrophic. In this specific variant, the posterior circulation, especially to the occipital lobe and mesencephalon, is provided by PComA [3].
Whether FPCA constitutes a risk factor for ischemic stroke (IS) is still controversial [4]. Several mechanisms of IS in FPCA have been identified. A recent study observed a more frequent small vessel disease-related IS and a lower frequency of embolic IS in FPCA configuration [5]. Yet, dissection of the ICA is an exceptional mechanism of IS in FPCA, with very few cases described to date.
Herein, we report a rare and misleading case of young-onset IS in the territory of PCA caused by extracranial and intracranial dissection of ICA.
A 46-year-old North African nonsmoker male patient presented to the neurology department of the National Institute Mongi Ben Hmida of Neurology, Tunis-Tunisia, 24 hours from acute onset of slurred speech, weakness, and impaired sensation in the left upper and lower limbs, as well as impaired visual field. [PMID 42823629] (Basic & clinical pharmacology & toxicology, 2026) Limitations of VKORC1 rs9934438 as a Surrogate Marker for Vitamin K Antagonist Dose Adjustment. VKORC1 genetic variants are major determinants of interindividual variability in vitamin K antagonist (VKA) dose requirements and are incorporated into several pharmacogenetic dosing guidelines. The promoter variant rs9923231 is considered the clinically relevant marker for genotype-guided VKA dosing. However, the intronic variant rs9934438 is sometimes used as a surrogate marker because it is assumed to be in strong linkage disequilibrium with rs9923231. We aimed to assess whether rs9934438 can reliably substitute rs9923231 in clinical practice. We conducted a retrospective, single-centre study including 939 patients who underwent pharmacogenetic testing. Both variants were genotyped using a TaqMan OpenArray custom panel. Concordance between rs9934438 and rs9923231 was evaluated, and the diagnostic performance of rs9934438 for predicting clinically relevant rs9923231 diplotypes was assessed. Although concordance was high overall, rs9934438 misclassified two patients who, according to rs9923231, required a reduced VKA dose, resulting in potential false-negative classifications. These findings indicate that, while rs9934438 provides informative results in most cases, it may fail to identify some patients requiring dose adjustment. Our results highlight the clinical implications of relying on surrogate markers in pharmacogenetic-guided VKA therapy and support the preferential use of rs9923231 to ensure accurate individualized dosing and optimize treatment safety.

paper_digests.title: Effects of apolipoprotein E and solute carrier organic anion transporter family member 1B1 gene polymorphisms on statin efficacy and safety in dyslipidemic patients.
paper_digests.dose_context: 20 mg atorvastatin daily or 10 mg rosuvastatin daily for 4 w

paragraphs.text: This study demonstrates that in this cohort of Han Chinese patients with dyslipidemia, the efficacy of atorvastatin is associated with ApoE genotypes, with E2 carriers achieving superior LDL-C reduction compared to E3 carriers. In contrast, no such association was observed for rosuvastatin. Regarding safety, the SLCO1B1 TC genotype did not confer a significantly increased risk of myopathy or hepatotoxicity over the TT genotype during low-to-moderate dose statin therapy. These findings provide evidence for the ApoE-guided selection of atorvastatin and support the relative safety of the SLCO1B1 TC genotype in this specific therapeutic context.

paragraphs.section: Distribution of solute carrier organic anion transporter family member 1B1 genotype by sex
paragraphs.text: Only two SLCO1B1 genotypes (TT and TC) were identified in this cohort, with the CC genotype not being detected. The TT genotype was predominant, with comparable frequencies in both males (85.90%) and females (82.90%). The χ2 test confirmed no statistically significant difference in genotype distribution between genders (P > 0.05). Detailed data are presented in Table 5.

paragraphs.section: Comparative analysis of lipid levels by apolipoprotein E genotype
paragraphs.text: The patient’s blood lipid levels were monitored after taking atorvastatin calcium 20 mg daily or rosuvastatin calcium 10 mg daily for 4 weeks. Significant intergroup differences in LDL-C levels were observed among ApoE genotypes in the atorvastatin cohort (F = 3.743, P = 0.026), with the E3 genotype exhibiting the highest levels (2.85 ± 1.00 mmol/l) and E2 the lowest (2.28 ± 0.96 mmol/l). TC showed borderline significance (P = 0.073), with numerically higher values in E3 versus E2/E4 genotypes. In contrast, no statistically significant differences in lipid parameters were observed across ApoE genotypes in the rosuvastatin group (P > 0.05). Complete data are presented in Table 6.

generated_answer: Based on the provided information and evidence, Vitanolix's potential adverse reactions may be influenced by genetic variations in vitamin D metabolism pathways. However, the evidence supporting these associations is currently insufficient or conflicting, particularly regarding spermatogenesis and sperm maturation. Therefore, while these genes should be included in a pharmacogenetic panel to predict patient response, further clinical validation is necessary before definitive conclusions can be drawn about their role in adverse reactions.

The genes involved in this pathway include VDR (Vitamin D Receptor), CYP2R1 (Cytochrome P450 Family 2 Subfamily R Member 1), CYP27A1 (Cytochrome P450 Family 2 Subfamily A Member 1), and CYP27B1. These genes are interconnected in the metabolism of vitamin D, with VDR being crucial for its biological effects and CYP enzymes involved in hydroxylation steps necessary for activation. Given that pharmacogenetic panels aim to identify genetic variations affecting drug response, including these genes would help predict how a patient might respond to Vitanolix based on their genetic makeup. Therefore, the genes to include are: VDR;CYP2R1;CYP27A1;CYP27B1.

[PMID 42883015 | PMC13663349 full text via pmc_xml] Testicular Expression of Vitamin-D Receptor and Vitamin-D-Metabolizing Enzymes (CYP2R1, CYP27A1, and CYP27B1) in Normal and Cryptorchid Horses. :: Cryptorchidism is a developmental defect in both animals and humans caused by failure of the testis to descend into the scrotal sac. In equines, this reproductive defect occurs in 5–8% of subjects [1] and can compromise fertility depending on whether one or both testes are retained in the abdominal cavity, inguinal canal, or in a subcutaneous position. Moreover, abdominal retention strongly affects fertility because spermatogenesis fails to occur at warm temperatures [2]. In general, the incidence of testicular retention in the abdomen is seen in 47–60% in equines, 90% in dogs, and 8% in humans [3]. The etiology of cryptorchidism is still under debate because a variety of genetic (polymorphism in different genes) and environmental risk factors (endocrine disruptors, extreme climate) are recognized as acting on the precise timing and coordination of the physiology of testicular descent [4]. Calcium [5] and testosterone [6] are two main regulators of male fertility. There is a strong relationship between calcium levels and male fertility because this ion is required in the testis for steroidogenesis [7], and spermatogenesis [8], while outside the gonad, is required for sperm motility, hyperactivation, and acrosome reaction [9]. In equines, cryptorchidism compromises fertility and reduces but not abolishes testosterone secretion [10]; furthermore, the residual capacity of the testicle to synthesize testosterone is responsible for undesirable sexual behaviors such as sexual excitement [11].
Vitamin D (VD) is a key regulator of systemic calcium homeostasis [12]. When produced by the skin, VD is inactive [13] and it requires a systemic activation, first in the microsome of the liver by two different 25-hydroxylases belonging to the cytochrome P450 family (CYP2R1 and CYP27A1) and then in the mitochondria of the proximal tubular cells of the kidney, where the 25OH-VD is 1α-hydroxylated to the hormonally active 1,25-dihydroxy-VD (1,25(OH)2VD) by CYP27B1 (1α-hydroxylase) [14]. VD acts on target cells by binding to its nuclear receptor (VDR) and heterodimerizing with the retinoid X receptor. The obtained complex behaves as a transcription factor to regulate target genes that contain a VD response element in their promoter. Recently, a VDR integrated in the plasma membrane has been discovered that explains the VD non-genomic action [15] that involves the activation of signaling molecules, the rapid generation of second messengers, and the opening of Ca2+ and Cl− channels [16].
The physiology of VD has not been studied in great depth in equines, and the few published studies suggest that VD may act differently for other species. It seems that equine skin is incapable of converting 7-dehydrocholesterol into VD after ultraviolet B-light exposure, so equines rely on their diet as primary sources of ergocalciferol, namely VD2 [17]. [PMID 31506976] (Hepatology (Baltimore, Md.), 2020) Vitamin D Receptor Activation in Liver Macrophages Ameliorates Hepatic Inflammation, Steatosis, and Insulin Resistance in Mice. Obesity-induced chronic inflammation is a key component in the pathogenesis of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and insulin resistance. Increased secretion of proinflammatory cytokines by macrophages in metabolic tissues promotes disease progression. In the diet-induced obesity (DIO) mouse model, activation of liver resident macrophages, or Kupffer cells (KCs), drives inflammatory responses, which recruits circulating macrophages and promotes fatty liver development, and ultimately contributes to impaired hepatic insulin sensitivity. Hepatic macrophages express the highest level of vitamin D receptors (VDRs) among nonparenchymal cells, whereas VDR expression is very low in hepatocytes. VDR activation exerts anti-inflammatory effects in immune cells. Here we found that VDR activation exhibits strong anti-inflammatory effects in mouse hepatic macrophages, including those isolated from DIO livers, and mice with genetic loss of Vdr developed spontaneous hepatic inflammation at 6 months of age. Under the chronic inflammation conditions of the DIO model, VDR activation by the vitamin D analog calcipotriol reduced liver inflammation and hepatic steatosis, significantly improving insulin sensitivity. The hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp revealed that VDR activation greatly increased the glucose infusion rate, while hepatic glucose production was remarkably decreased. Glucose uptake in muscle and adipose did not show similar effects, suggesting that improved hepatic insulin sensitivity is the primary contributor to the beneficial effects of VDR activation. paragraphs.text: Spermatocytes expressed VDR and CYP2R1, CYP27A1, and CYP27B1 in the scrotal testis of unilateral cryptorchid equines and in the testis of normal stallions. Since VDR and CYP2R1 showed a similar staining intensity in spermatocytes and spermatogonia, it can be assumed that these epitopes are constitutive components of equine spermatogenetic cells. Compared to spermatogonia, spermatocytes contained additional VD-activating enzymes such as CYP27A1 and CYP27B1. The presence of these two enzymes was more evident in control equines then in scrotal testes of unilateral cryptorchids. This finding may be related to a high fertility of control then unilateral cryptorchid equines. VDR has been detected in spermatocytes of rats [43] and roosters [44]. In human testes, spermatocytes have a high expressi

During spermiogenesis, all morphologically distinguishable types of spermatids (round and elongated spermatids) expressed VDR, CYP2R1, CYP27A1, and CYP27B1 in control equines. These findings evidence that an extrarenal activation of VD occurs in equines and that it may be important for spermatogenesis and sperm maturation. Our immunohistochemical results are consistent with those reported in men, whose round and elongated spermatids express VDR- and VD-activating enzymes [21].

It is interesting to note that, in the scrotal testes of animals with unilateral cryptorchidism, VDR, CYP2R1, and CYP27B1 were found only in round spermatids, whilst CYP27A1 was never detected. The comparison of these findings with those that we observed in the healthy control equines and by Blomberg Jensen et al. [21] in humans, suggests that the normal maturation of spermatids requires VDR- and VD-activating enzymes and that the spermiogenesis occurring in the scrotal testes of animals with unilateral cryptorchidism has an altered VD metabolism. In addition, the absence of the CYP27A1 may be a biomarker of defective molecular composition of equine spermatids. The results demonstrated that equine testes express the genes coding for VDR- and for VD-activating enzymes (Figure 4) and that cryptorchidism affects mRNA levels of the investigated genes. The amount of VDR mRNA was not correlated to the localization of the retained testicle. The corresponding protein was also expressed in the equine testis with a reduced level in the abdominal-retained testicle compared to its contralateral scrotal testicle, while the expression in the inguinal-retained testicle was like the contralateral scrotal one.

paragraphs.text: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is a transitional state between normal aging and dementia, and genetic factors may influence progression. This transporter has a broad substrate profile and is able to transport substrates against their concentration gradient, making it an interesting target for brain drug delivery. However, the molecular identity of this transporter remains unknown. Recent studies have indicated that the two proteins TM7SF3 and LHFPL6 might be components of this transporter. The present study aimed to investigate the roles of TM7SF3 and LHFPL6 in the H+/OC antiporter function to advance understanding of its molecular identity and potential in CNS drug delivery. CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing was used to generate three hCMEC/D3 knockout (KO) cell lines: TM7SF3 KO (TM-KO), LHFPL6 KO (LH-KO), and a double KO of TM7SF3 and LHFPL6 (TMLH-KO). The uptake of pyrilamine analogue (EDMPG) and [3H]-pyrilamine was assessed in wild type (WT) and KO lines. Out of 392 patients, 323 responded to the treatment and 17.6% discontinued either due to insufficient response or intolerable adverse events (AEs). GA genotype was more frequent in non-responder group (P ˂ 0.001). Maximum pain responders (≥50%) in combination with the lowest incidence of AEs were observed in the GG group, whereas partial responders belonged to GA genotype and with the highest frequency of somnolence (83.6%) and dizziness (69.9%). Overall, 72.5% patients with GA genotype experienced AEs (P ˂ 0.001). In conclusion, clinical outcomes of gabapentinoids are influenced by LAT1 rs4240803 polymorphism and population pharmacogenetics should be considered to evaluate the maximum potential of gabapentinoids in the management of neuropathic pain.

[PMID 42912715] (Neuroendocrinology, 2026) The contribution of PLCB1 and VDR gene variants to susceptibility of central precocious puberty in Hubei Han Chinese girls: Integrating case-control evidence with meta-analysis. Central precocious puberty (CPP) is a prevalent pediatric endocrine disorder resulting from the premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis. PLCB1 acts downstream of the KISS1/GPR54 signaling pathway to mediate gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secretion, a key event in pubertal initiation. Moreover, VDR is widely expressed in breast tissue, modulates glandular development, and low serum vitamin D levels have been associated with an elevated risk of CPP. This research aimed to investigate the association between genetic variants in the PLCB1 and VDR genes and CPP susceptibility in Hubei Han Chinese girls. A total of 384 CPP girls and 422 healthy girls from Hubei province were enrolled in this case-control study, which targeted three PLCB1 gene variants (rs932491, rs2235613, rs708910) and three VDR gene variants (rs731236, rs7975232, rs1544410). A comprehensive meta-analysis integrating this study and existing literature was subsequently conducted. For the rs708910, the A allele and AA genotype were identified as protective factors against CPP risk. For the rs7975232, the C allele and CC genotype were significantly associated with a reduced risk of CPP. The subsequent meta-analysis confirmed that both rs708910 and rs7975232 were robustly linked to CPP susceptibility in the Chinese population. The PLCB1 gene rs708910 and VDR gene rs7975232 may represent potential risk-associated variants for CPP in Han Chinese girls. These findings warrant validation in future large-scale, multi-ethnic cohort studies.

T2DM is a complex disorder, caused by genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors in addition to medical conditions and lifestyle, which also contribute to the development of DM.4, 5 Patients with T2DM display variable degrees of insulin resistance, altered insulin secretion, increased hepatic glucose production, and inflammation.5, 6 Moreover, individuals with T2DM are prone to infections due to impaired immune response. For example, mucormycosis, a severe fungal infection, occurs frequently in patients with diabetes.7
Vitamin D (VD) is one of the factors that contribute to increased risk for T2DM.8, 9, 10 Recent studies further support the role of VD signaling and metabolic regulation in glucose homeostasis and metabolic disorders, highlighting its broader systemic effects beyond calcium metabolism.11 VD plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including calcium and phosphate homeostasis, regulation of cell differentiation and proliferation, immune function, insulin secretion, blood pressure and neuromuscular function.12, 13, 14, 15 Numerous medical conditions have been linked to VD deficiency such as obesity, gastrointestinal, hypertension, cardiovascular risk, dyslipidemia, autoimmune diseases, cancer in addition to mental health and neurological disorders, including multiple sclerosis and Alzheimer's, suggesting that VD deficiency is a risk factor for these disorders.16, 17, 18 Furthermore, our previous research have shown an association between genetic polymorphisms in CYP2R1, CYP27B1, and other VD metabolism-related genes with the development of schizophrenia.19

paragraphs.section: Genotype and allele frequencies of the four SNPs
paragraphs.text: Based on the findings obtained, two SNPs: CYP2R1 (rs10741657; A > G and rs1074165; G > A), showed statistically significant differences between the two groups. Furthermore, the genotype frequency differences, particularly the higher prevalence of heterozygous genotypes among patients, could reflect an association with disease susceptibility. Specifically, the G allele of rs10741657 and the A allele of rs1074165 were enriched among patients and may be associated with increased disease risk.

paragraphs.section: Association of gene polymorphisms with T2DM risk
paragraphs.text: For CYP2R1 (rs10741657; A > G), the number of individuals with the GG genotype was low in both groups (6 controls vs 9 patients). The AG genotype was found to be significantly associated with increased risk of developing diabetes (OR = 3.69; 95% CI: 2.27–6.00), whereas the rare GG genotype showed an elevated but non-significant crude estimate (OR = 2.44; 95% CI: 0.84–7.11) (Table 2). Moreover, carriers of the G allele were significantly more likely to develop the disease than those with the A allele (OR = 2.59; 95% CI: 1.77–3.77; P < 0.01) (Table 3).

paragraphs.section: Association of gene polymorphisms with T2DM risk
paragraphs.text: For CYP2R1 (rs1074165; G > A), because the AA genotype was absent in controls, its OR was not estimated without continuity correction; the genotype was retained descriptively. The GA genotype showed a strong association with the disease relative to the GG genotype (OR = 4.27; 95% CI: 2.22–8.22) (Table 2). Carriers of the A allele were almost 5-folds more likely to develop diabetes compared to controls (OR = 4.68; 95% CI: 2.51–8.72, P < 0.01).

paper_digests.summary: The paper reports on the association of CYP2R1 gene polymorphisms with type 2 diabetes mellitus in Jordanian individuals. Two SNPs (rs10741657 and rs1074165) showed statistically significant differences between cases and controls, indicating an increased risk for developing diabetes among carriers of the G allele at rs10741657 and A allele at rs1074165. No actionable pharmacogenetic guidelines are mentioned for vitanolix.

However, the CYP27B1 rs4646536 polymorphism and HBP did not maintain significance across any model.

The uptake of pyrilamine analogue (EDMPG) and [3H]-pyrilamine was assessed in wild type (WT) and KO lines. The EDMPG uptake was significantly reduced in TM-, LH-, and TMLH-KO cells, suggesting that TM7SF3 and LHFPL6 contribute to the H+/OC antiporter function. [PMID 33190395] (Basic & clinical pharmacology & toxicology, 2021) Influence of single nucleotide polymorphism of LAT1 on therapeutic response to gabapentinoids in Pakistani patients with neuropathic pain. Gabapentinoids are substrate of L-type amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) for distribution across the blood-brain barrier. The present study aimed to evaluate the effect of LAT1 rs4240803 genetic polymorphism on the clinical efficacy and tolerability of gabapentinoids in Pakistani patients with neuropathic pain. Three-hundred and ninety-two patients were recruited, genotyped for SNP rs4240803, and followed up for eight weeks to evaluate the clinical response to gabapentinoids in terms of pain relief, inadequate response, and the emergence of adverse events. LAT1 rs4240803 GG, GA, and AA genotype frequency were 33.42%, 47.96% and 18.62%, respectively. Out of 392 patients, 323 responded to the treatment and 17.6% discontinued either due to insufficient response or intolerable adverse events (AEs). GA genotype was more frequent in non-responder group (P ˂ 0.001). Maximum pain responders (≥50%) in combination with the lowest incidence of AEs were observed in the GG group, whereas partial responders belonged to GA genotype and with the highest frequency of somnolence (83.6%) and dizziness (69.9%). Overall, 72.5% patients with GA genotype experienced AEs (P ˂ 0.001). In conclusion, clinical outcomes of gabapentinoids are influenced by LAT1 rs4240803 polymorphism and population pharmacogenetics should be considered to evaluate the maximum potential of gabapentinoids in the management of neuropathic pain.

paragraphs.text: The putative proton/organic cation (H+/OC) antiporter has been shown to mediate transport of CNS drug compounds like oxycodone and pyrilamine across the blood-brain barrier (BBB). This transporter has a broad substrate profile and is able to transport substrates against their concentration gradient, making it an interesting target for brain drug delivery. However, the molecular identity of this transporter remains unknown. Recent studies have indicated that the two proteins TM7SF3 and LHFPL6 might be components of this transporter. The present study aimed to investigate the roles of TM7SF3 and LHFPL6 in the H+/OC antiporter function to advance understanding of its molecular identity and potential in CNS drug delivery. paragraphs.text: Gabapentinoids are substrate of L-type amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) for distribution across the blood-brain barrier. The present study aimed to evaluate the effect of LAT1 rs4240803 genetic polymorphism on the clinical efficacy and tolerability of gabapentinoids in Pakistani patients with neuropathic pain. Three-hundred and ninety-two patients were recruited, genotyped for SNP rs4240803, and followed up for eight weeks to evaluate the clinical response to gabapentinoids in terms of pain relief, inadequate response, and the emergence of adverse events. LAT1 rs4240803 GG, GA, and AA genotype frequency were 33.42%, 47.96% and 18.62%, respectively. [PMID 42396658 | PMC13336519 full text via pmc_xml] ABCG2 transporter: Structural and functional associations with gout (Review). :: Hyperuricemia (HUA) and its clinical manifestation, gout, a major metabolic disease, are recognized by the World Health Organization as major global health challenges (1). Gout is considered to be a major cause of disability and is closely associated with metabolic syndrome comorbidities (2,3). Fundamentally, gout is a disorder of urate homeostasis that occurs when serum urate concentrations exceed their physiological solubility limit (4). Physiologically, HUA is defined by elevated serum urate levels [typically >6.8 mg/dl (400 µmol/l)] (5-7). Serum urate homeostasis can be influenced by sex hormones, with men typically exhibiting higher concentrations (5.0-7.0 mg/dl) than premenopausal women (4.0-6.0 mg/dl) (5,8,9). Elevated urate levels promote the formation of monosodium urate crystals, which deposit in joints and soft tissues, triggering an inflammatory cascade characteristic of gouty arthritis (10). Globally, the prevalence of gout is rising, with cases projected to increase by >70% from 2020 to 2050, reaching ~95.8 million (11). This trend is mainly driven by dietary transitions toward purine-rich and fructose-laden foods, as well as by increasing obesity rates and aging populations (3,12,13).
The impact of HUA extends beyond human health to animal husbandry. In poultry, uric acid is the primary nitrogenous waste product, with serum concentrations typically ranging between 5 and 7 mg/dl; however, this can exceed 20 mg/dl under conditions of renal failure. This sharp elevation precipitates visceral gout, a fatal condition that results in high mortality rates and substantial economic losses due to reduced productivity (14,15). Research using animal models has enhanced the mechanistic understanding of the disease, as uricase-deficient mice exhibit sustained serum urate levels of 5-6 mg/dl, whereas wild-type mice require higher inducer doses to develop persistent HUA leading to gouty arthritis and renal injury, thereby closely mirroring human pathophysiology (16-18). Untreated conditions can cause chronic joint damage, tophus formation, and increased risks of kidney and cardiovascular diseases (4,19).
Urate homeostasis is maintained through a delicate balance between production and excretion. Uric acid production arises from the metabolism of purines derived from dietary sources (red meat and seafood), as well as endogenous purine nucleotide turnover, with the final conversion to uric acid catalyzed by xanthine oxidase (8,20,21). Nutritional factors serve a pivotal role in urate metabolism; high purine and fructose intake, as well as high-protein/high-calcium diets in poultry, can lead to urate overproduction and precipitate HUA (22,23). However, most patients with gout experience impaired urate excretion rather than overproduction as the main underlying disorder (2). [PMID 42930531] (Medical sciences (Basel, Switzerland), 2026) The Human Urate Transportosome: Evolutionary Dynamics, Molecular Mechanisms, and Pharmacogenetic Perspectives. Background: The hominoid loss of urate oxidase (uricase) represents a classic evolutionary trade-off, shifting uric acid (UA) from a metabolic waste product to a potent physiological modulator. In modern metabolic environments, however, this adaptation drives hyperuricemia and gout, transforming UA into a primary pathological substrate. Objective: This review aims to dissect the molecular architecture and biophysical networks of the renal and intestinal urate transportosome, delineate the dual intracellular/extracellular "urate paradox," and synthesize genotype-based pharmacogenetic strategies to achieve personalized clinical management. Mechanistic Insights: During the Miocene epoch, inactivating pseudogenization of the UOX gene fixed a novel metabolic phenotype characterized by fructose-driven lipid deposition and enhanced antioxidant protection. Structurally, systemic urate homeostasis is strictly governed by a macromolecular interactome assembled by the four-domain scaffold protein PDZK1 on the epithelial apical membrane. Pathogenic gain-of-function variants in reabsorption facilitators (SLC22A12/URAT1, SLC2A9/GLUT9) or loss-of-function mutations in the efflux pump (ABCG2/BCRP) disrupt this delicate vector kinetics. Within the extracellular space, soluble urate acts as a critical hydrophilic radical scavenger. Paradoxically, upon URAT1/GLUT9-mediated internalization or intracellular supersaturation, intracellular urate triggers a pro-oxidant cascade mediated by NADPH oxidase (NOX4) activation and mitochondrial electron transport chain decoupling. paragraphs.text: The ABCG2 Q141K variant has wide-ranging clinical implications because it impairs ABCG2 transporter function, thereby contributing to HUA and gout, and influencing drug disposition, disease progression and the therapeutic response. Clinical data indicate that carriers are more likely to progress to tophaceous gout and experience increased flare frequency, reflecting its role in sustaining urate burden (82). A hallmark of Q141K variant-associated disease is the variability in treatment response, as carriers often exhibit reduced efficacy of uricosuric agents, such as benzbromarone and lesinurad, due to impaired intestinal and renal urate excretion that cannot be fully restored pharmacologically (8,129). [PMID 31999635] (Journal of infection in developing countries, 2018) Impact of IL28B genetic variant's and viral genotype on treatment outcome of hepatitis C infected patients. Viral genotype and variation in host genes involved in the immune response may predict the treatment response in patients infected with HCV. The present study was designed to determine the distribution pattern of HCV and host genotypes in Chronic Hepatitis C (CHC) patients and their association with virological response and other risk factors. Two hundred and fifty (n = 250) HCV positive patients were included in the study. HCV and Interleukin 28B (IL28B) genotyping was carried out by PCR-RFLP. Viral genotype 3 was the predominant genotype seen in 187 (74.8%) patients. Wild genotype predominated in rs12979860, rs12980275 and rs8099917 SNP of IL28B gene. A significant difference was found in end stage virological response (EVR) between HCV genotype 1 infected patients with wild and variant genotype for rs12980275 and rs8099917 SNPs respectively (P < 0.05). On multivariate analysis all the SNPs were found to be associated with each other (P < 0.05) with rs12980275 SNP associated with history of Jaundice (P < 0.05). Viral genotype 3 was significantly associated with age (< 50 years) and rapid virological response (RVR) while as viral genotype 1 was significantly associated with history of surgery on multivariate analysis (P < 0.05). The viral genotype and IL28B polymorphisms are important factors to personalize antiviral therapy of patients with CHC.
[PMID 38406928] (Journal of Ayub Medical College, Abbottabad : JAMC, 2023) Predictive Potential Of Il28b Gene In Hcv Patients, Resistant To Daclatasvir And Sofosbuvir In KPK Population. Recently various combinations of direct acting antivirals (DAAs) have been tried successfully. The Sofosbuvir + Daclatasvir combination has been used with promising results. Recently, resistance has been noticed against DAAs. Therefore, polymorphism at particular sites in the interleukin 28B gene are under study to find possible association with resistance. This study was aimed at finding out any association of SNPs rs8099917 and rs12979860 (IL28B gene) with response and resistance to treatment in HCV genotype 3 patients in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. This cross sectional, Analytical study was conducted at Gastroenterology/hepatology OPD of Prime Teaching Hospital, Peshawar Medical College. Collected Samples were stored at -20o C in PCR Lab of the College. DNA extraction and genotyping was carried out at BJ Molecular Biology Lab in Rawalpindi. Data was analyzed by using SPSS version 21. Chi-Square Test was used to see the statistically significant differences between rs8099917 T/G and rs12979860 T/C model. In the IL28-B gene, single nucleotide polymorphism at rs12979860 T/C model, we observed that there are 37.5% CC homozygous, 12.5% TT homozygous and 50% CT heterozygous genotypes in resistant patients and 42.85% CC homozygous, 28.57% TT and 28.57% CT genotype in responder group. In rs12979860 T/C model, genotype of IL28-B in the responder and resistant group significantly varies at p-value =0.00572. We conclude that in SNP at rs12979860, CC genotype is associated with clearance of HCV, while CT genotype was more prevalent in the resistant group and associated with chronicity.

[PMID 42801138 | PMC13615476 full text via pmc_xml] Allelic Frequency of Single-Nucleotide Polymorphisms in CYP2C9, VKORC1, and CYP4F2 Genetic Variants in Patients With Mechanical Heart Valves on Acenocoumarol Drug Therapy. :: Patients with mechanical heart valve replacement need to take lifelong anticoagulation therapy. This is to prevent blood clots from forming on the valve [1,2]. Mechanical heart valves are more likely to get blood clots than tissue heart valves. Mechanical valves are more durable but require lifelong anticoagulation. Tissue valves do not require lifelong anticoagulation but wear out in 10-15 years. Thus, mechanical valves are preferred for younger patients, while tissue valves are better for older patients. The anticoagulant therapy helps reduce the risk of stroke, valve thrombosis, and other complications. Vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), such as warfarin and acenocoumarol, are widely used anticoagulants after heart valve replacement.
Traditional VKAs, such as warfarin and acenocoumarol, are the only FDA-approved oral anticoagulants for preventing valve thrombosis in mechanical heart valves. New oral anticoagulants (NOACs) or direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), such as dabigatran, apixaban, and rivaroxaban, are not FDA-approved for patients with mechanical heart valve replacements. In fact, they are strongly contraindicated for this purpose. Early clinical trials (e.g., the RE-ALIGN trial for dabigatran) showed that NOACs are associated with significantly higher rates of complications, including blood clots on the valve, strokes, and major bleeding, compared to older medications [3,4].
Acenocoumarol has a narrow therapeutic index; small changes in dosage can cause bleeding or thrombotic complications [5]. The acenocoumarol dosage can vary from person to person, depending on environmental factors and genetics. The main enzyme that metabolizes acenocoumarol in the liver is cytochrome P450 2C9 (CYP2C9), which is highly polymorphic. There are three main forms: CYP2C9*1 (normal or wild allele), CYP2C9*2, and CYP2C9*3. People with CYP2C9*2 and *3 variants have reduced enzyme activity, so they need lower doses of acenocoumarol.
However, there is limited data from Central India on how genetic variability affects acenocoumarol dosage. The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) guidelines recommend genotype-based dosing for warfarin [6], but there is no specific recommendation for acenocoumarol. However, the Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group (DPWG) has recommended that patients with the VKORC1 (c.-1639G>A) AA genotype should be given 50% of the standard initial dose of acenocoumarol and undergo more frequent international normalized ratio (INR) monitoring. As per the DPWG, there are currently no recommendations for acenocoumarol dosing based on CYP2C9 genotypes [7]. This means that the patient's genetic profile should be considered for precision dosing of the VKA. It is essential to get the right dosage to prevent complications. An overdose of acenocoumarol can cause bleeding, and an underdose can cause blood clots. By considering a patient's genetic variability, more effective and safer anticoagulation therapy can be provided [8
[PMID 42835306 | PMC13635174 full text via pmc_xml] Pharmacogenetics in pediatric cardiology. :: With emerging techniques that can deliver precision therapeutics to the individual patient, pediatric cardiac patients may stand to benefit the most from adoption of pharmacogenetic guidance, given the specialized drug therapy required in the management of this unique population. Although strides have been made in pediatric drug labeling (1), labeling for pediatric cardiovascular therapeutics remains significantly inadequate (2). Alarmingly, at least 80% of pediatric cardiac patients receive at least one off-label medication and nearly 30% receive three or more (3–5). As a result, insufficient therapeutic response and adverse events rates are common among children, adolescents, and young adults with congenital and acquired heart disease, emphasizing the urgent need for prospective evaluation of drug safety and effectiveness in this population (6–8).
Traditional drug development and optimization rely on broad, largely homogenous cohorts and, subsequently, extrapolate the data to individual patients. In pediatric cardiology, this problem is amplified, as evidence is almost exclusively from adults with acquired cardiovascular disease, as opposed to congenital heart disease (CHD), and is then applied to children of varying ages, developmental stages, and underlying pathophysiology. However, strides to address the knowledge gaps in the developmental trajectories of drug disposition, namely drug metabolism (9–12) and transporters (13) have been accomplished. Unfortunately, data on the impact of genetic variation on drug disposition and response in pediatric cardiovascular patients is limited.
Before precision-based care strategies, such as pharmacogenetic-guided dosing, can be effectively implemented, pediatric cardiac providers must first appreciate both pharmacologic properties of the administered drug and the unique patient factors that could potentially influence the dose-exposure-response relationship for that individual pediatric cardiac patient. Many of the factors have previously been described in several comprehensive reviews (14–19). Importantly, sources of variability in drug disposition (i.e., the dose-exposure relationship) should be defined before linking differences in drug response to genetic variation in drug targets. Genetic variation in the protein(s) responsible for drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion is illustrated in Figure 1. Developmental ontogeny, which describes age-related changes in drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters, further complicates matters (19). Although additional prospectively-generated data in the pediatric cardiac patient is urgently needed, there is emerging evidence to support pharmacogenetic-informed treatment guidelines, which will be discussed herein.

We observe that the *1/*2 genotype frequency of CYP2C9*2 and VKORC1-1639 are approximately equal to those reported in other North Indian population studies [2,13,14]. The CYP4F2 gene encodes vitamin K oxidase, an enzyme responsible for metabolizing vitamin K. The CYP4F2*3 variant (V433M, rs2108622) reduces enzyme activity, leading to increased hepatic vitamin K levels. This mechanism counteracts the effects of VKORC1 variants by increasing the vitamin K available for carboxylation, thereby requiring higher VKA doses [16,17].

In our study, we observed a 32% heterozygous (*1/*3) and 8% homozygous mutant (*3/*3) frequency for CYP4F2*3. This represents a substantial proportion of patients (40%) who may require higher acenocoumarol doses than predicted by CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotyping alone. Previous studies from North India did not include CYP4F2 genotyping, making our study the first to report these frequencies in Central India [2,11,12].

[PMID 34376788 | PMC9267777 full text via pmc_xml] Appraisal and development of evidence-based clinical decision support to enable perioperative pharmacogenomic application. :: Adverse drug events (ADEs) and drug inefficacy remain challenging problems within the perioperative setting.1–4 Patients’ fears surrounding receiving anesthesia are one of the greatest contributors to perioperative anxiety5, and providers are acutely aware of unintended anesthetic and pain medication complications. Unpredictability is affected by a complex interplay of heterogeneous diseases being treated, rapidly changing states of organ function, critical illness, and patient factors, including genetic factors.
Probably the best-known perioperative pharmacogenetic example is malignant hyperthermia—a syndrome recognized since the 1960s6. Various genetic polymorphisms in the RYR1 and CACNA1S genes predispose individuals to this syndrome, which presents as a life-threatening hypermetabolic response to succinylcholine and certain volatile anesthetics7. Identifying a patient at increased risk for this condition through attaining a family history, and if necessary, additional testing, is standard practice and essential for medication decisions, suggesting preemptive pharmacogenomic testing may prove beneficial. Outside of anesthesiology, many additional examples of genetic-related medication risk stratification have been recently identified and incorporated into clinical practice, including HLA-B*57:01 testing for hypersensitivity to abacavir and HLA-B*1502 testing for risk of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome with carbamazepine use8–14. Despite implementation of genetic information to inform prescribing in these other medical settings, the routine use of such information within anesthesiology and critical care remains almost nonexistent.
While a number of potential barriers may explain this15, 16, one of the most frequently-cited reasons is the paucity of guidance around available evidence to support clinical pharmacogenomic actionability for most common medications used by anesthesiologists and critical care physicians. This means that any effort to consider whether a translational gap exists between discovery and clinical practice for anesthesia requires an appraisal and integration of the evidence, and development of straightforward decision supports to enable clinical consideration. Using a comprehensive appraisal and clinical decision-support development methodology that our group has applied in other subspecialty settings, including cardiology and oncology17–19, we sought to interrogate the clinical relevance of current pharmacogenomic evidence and enable potential clinical translation of such knowledge for anesthesia, critical care, and acute pain medicine in this original research study. We hypothesized that the clinical relevance of pharmacogenomic evidence for perioperative medications will be considerable and will comprise an evidence base that justifies future prospective clinical examination of pharmacogenomics in this field.

[PMID 42794754 | PMC13607192 full text via pmc_xml] Estimating the Prevalence of Malignant Hyperthermia Susceptibility Based on Causative RYR1 and CACNA1S Variants. :: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare but potentially fatal complication of general anesthesia, caused by uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. Clinical manifestations of MH include acidosis, hypercapnia, tachycardia, hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, compartment syndrome, rhabdomyolysis with subsequent elevation of serum creatine kinase (CK), hyperkalemia with the risk of cardiac arrhythmia or even cardiac arrest, and myoglobinuria with the risk of renal failure. In almost all patients, the first signs of MH (hypercapnia, tachycardia, and tachypnea) appear in the operating room; however, symptoms may also emerge during the early postoperative period [1]. For anesthesiologists and intensivists, MH is of particular practical importance, since timely recognition of the risk allows triggering agents to be avoided and safe anesthetic protocols to be used.
Estimating the prevalence of MHS is more difficult than estimating the frequency of MH crises themselves. A clinical crisis occurs only when genetic predisposition, exposure to a triggering agent, and sufficient individual susceptibility coincide. As a result, the reported frequency of MH episodes is inevitably lower than the genetic frequency of MHS. Additional reasons for this discrepancy include incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity, the absence of prior exposure to volatile anesthetics in some carriers, difficulties in diagnosing mild or atypical episodes, and the limited availability of contracture testing and functional variant validation.
The exact incidence of MH is unknown because of incomplete ascertainment of abortive forms of the syndrome. According to various sources, the incidence in children is approximately 1 in 3000–15,000 general anesthetics, and in adults approximately 1 in 50,000–100,000 general anesthetics, whereas the estimated genetic prevalence may be as high as 1 in 2000–3000 in the general population [2,3,4].
The central hypothesis of this article is that the carrier frequency of pathogenic and likely pathogenic RYR1 variants associated with MHS exceeds the clinical frequency of reported MH crises [5]. This discrepancy should be regarded not as a contradiction but as an expected consequence of the pharmacogenetic nature of MHS: the genetic risk is present prior to exposure, whereas the clinical phenotype manifests only under specific external conditions.
Variants in RYR1 account for approximately 76% of MHS cases, whereas CACNA1S accounts for approximately 1% [6].
RYR1 encodes the ryanodine receptor and represents a large calcium-release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum that is central to excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle. In MHS, most well-established causative RYR1 variants are missense substitutions that alter channel regulation and increase the probability of pathological calcium release in response to triggering anesthetics. paragraphs.text: Until now, pharmacogenomic results have been infrequently utilized in anesthesia and critical care clinical settings33, 34. Barriers to clinical use not only included prior skepticism about the readiness of evidence for clinical utility examinations, but also lack of available genetic testing and reimbursement, concerns about test turnaround times, lack of integration into clinical workflows/electronic medical records, and inadequate decision support for providers unfamiliar with genomics15, 16, 35, 36. This latter point—including confusion around recommendations for many pharmacogenomic drug/gene pairs—has likely slowed the adoption of pharmacogenomic testing in anesthesia, as it has in other areas. For example, preemptive RYR1 screening is not endorsed by the Malignant Hyperthermia Assoc

Original CDS summaries for each potential genotype associated with each potential clinical consequence were then developed for each of the 18 medications. Screen shots of genotype-specific CDS summaries for sevoflurane and succinylcholine, as examples, are shown in Figure 3. The remaining CDS summaries are available in Supplemental File 4. One composite summary was written for all of the NSAIDs (celecoxib, diclofenac, flurbiprofen, ibuprofen, and piroxicam as associated with CYP2C9), and one composite summary was written for the six anesthetics (desflurane, enflurane, halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, and succinylcholine as associated with RYR1 and CACNA1S mutations).
